mappings.note: Enslaved Africans on American plantations - the destructive human cost of the colonial trade, LO-6, not LO-5, which is about connection as such.
Why Indian cotton exports to Britain collapsed - tariffs protecting British industry, LO-6's damage to colonised livelihoods.
The consequence for Indian weavers of losing the British market - LO-6.
Falling European household incomes after the First World War - one of the changes that transformed the world, LO-4.
Women taking men's jobs during the war - a wartime social transformation, LO-4.
Which power stayed out of the First World War - LO-4, the war as the era's transforming event.
Where the Great Depression began - LO-4.
An aim of the post-war international economic system - the machinery of global interconnectedness, LO-5, rather than LO-4's description of change.
Henry Ford and the assembly line - a transformation in production, LO-4.
Bretton Woods, 1944 - the founding of the post-war global economic order, LO-5.
The IMF and World Bank as Bretton Woods' outcome - LO-5's 'to the present day'.
Why MNCs moved to China - present-day interconnectedness, LO-5.
British industrial growth pulling in food imports - trade binding regions together, LO-5.
US veto over IMF and World Bank decisions - how the global order is governed today, LO-5.
Where the First World War was mainly fought - LO-4.
African exploration tied to conquest and resource extraction - LO-6, the colonial impact, not LO-5's neutral connection.
Ancient travellers seeking knowledge and opportunity - the pre-modern end of LO-5.
Potatoes, maize and chillies crossing to the Old World - the Columbian exchange, LO-5's pre-modern interconnectedness.
The Irish famine deaths of 1845-49 under British rule - livelihoods destroyed, LO-6. NOTE: the stem says 10,000,000 dead; the textbook figure is about 1,000,000.
19th-century European migration to America - people flows as interconnectedness, LO-5, not LO-4.
